questions.question: Inside an instance method, what does this refer to?
options: The object the method was called on
questions.explanation: this is a reference to the current object, the one on which the method is running.

questions.question: class Cab { String city; Cab(String city) { city = city; } } Why does new Cab("Pune").city stay null?
options: The parameter is assigned to itself, so the field is never set
Strings cannot be assigned in constructors
questions.explanation: Both names mean the parameter. Writing this.city = city stores the value in the field.

questions.question: class Box { int n; Box() { this(5); n++; } Box(int n) { this.n = n; } } ... System.out.println(new Box().n); What prints?
questions.explanation: this(5) sets n to 5, then the rest of the no-argument constructor adds 1, giving 6.

questions.question: Box() { n = 2; this(7); } Why does this constructor fail to compile?
options: The call to this(...) must be the first statement
questions.explanation: A this(...) or super(...) call is only allowed as the first statement of a constructor.

questions.question: Why can't this be used inside a static method?
options: A static method runs without any current object
It can be used if the class is public
questions.explanation: Static methods are called on the class, so there is no object for this to point to.

questions.question: class Cart { int items; Cart add() { items++; return this; } } ... System.out.println(new Cart().add().add().add().items); What prints?
questions.explanation: Each add() returns the same object, so all three calls increase the same items field to 3.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a valid use of this?
options: Passing the current object to a method
Returning the current object from a method
Calling another constructor of the same class
Calling a static method as this() from main
questions.explanation: this() is only for calling another constructor from a constructor, and main is static, so it has no this at all.

questions.question: class Ride { boolean check(Ride r) { return this == r; } } ... Ride a = new Ride(); Ride b = new Ride(); System.out.println(a.check(b) + " " + b.check(b)); What prints?
questions.explanation: a.check(b) compares two different objects. In b.check(b), this and r are the same object.

questions.question: Can a constructor contain both this(...) and super(...) calls?
options: No, only one of them can be the first statement
questions.explanation: Both must be the first statement, so a constructor can hold only one of them.

questions.question: class Van { Van() { this(1); } Van(int s) { this(); } } What goes wrong?
questions.explanation: The compiler detects that the two constructors call each other in a loop and rejects the code.
